en: Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Bodhiruci, who temporarily manifested as the Nine-Eyed Deva Kāñcanaprabha:
Those who first wish to perform this rite should not carve the image [from wood], but rather cast it from white *ge* (karpūra), copper, or sandalwood.
As for the use of cypress, pine, and other woods when constructing [the image], one must not exceed a height of three, five, or seven inches on any single day or night.
When painting with colors, do not use animal glue; instead, use fragrant juices or the sap of trees.
The golden-hued body stands upright with three heads, each face having three eyes, totaling nine eyes. The bridge of the nose extends upward...
The neck is level with the shoulders, and it is encircled by a skin-crawling insect. It has four arms: the upper left hand holds a *modaka* (joy-pellet), and the upper right hand holds a radish root;
the lower left and right hands form the *mūdrā* of the Root [Mantra]. He wears white robes and treads upon a golden mountain.

Furthermore, when fashioning [the image], do not allow miscellaneous people to see it. Burn fragrant incense and remain pure, abstaining from the five pungent roots (*pañca-garaka*). Once the carving of the image is completed, [place it] in a clean [location].
Within the chamber, one should establish an altar, square and circular, measuring one and a half cubits in length and breadth and one finger-breadth in height, and smear it with yellow earth;
if one does not dare to do so, one may make a wooden altar. The image should face west while the master faces east.
Two precious vases are placed thereon, and fresh flowers are offered while burning renowned incense; if no renowned incense is available, burn *agaru* (sandalwood) and aloeswood within the chamber.

Various offerings such as parched grain, milk porridge, *modaka* cakes, clarified butter, honey, radish roots, fried cakes, and confections should be presented as daily offerings at the three times of day.
If the mantra-practitioner is a layperson, they should wear white garments; those who are impure must not be employed, nor should they be used for making offerings.
One must not blow on the fire with the mouth, but use a fan instead. Those who lack faith shall perish.
One should not approach those who have given birth, householders, male or female slaves, women, those with provisional names, monks, śrāmaṇeras, or disciples.
One must not touch their pure mats, seats, buckets, or ladles. Their requisites must be pure.

The mantra master, having aroused great compassion for all sentient beings and being pure both internally and externally, shall sit upon a seat made of *kuśa* grass according to the prescribed dwellings; this is the natural law (*dharmatā*).
To recite the fundamental great mantra of the Nine-Eyed Deva, who manifests as the golden Kanavati:
first, perform the outer binding with both hands and join the two index fingers; the mantra is as follows:
Namo cudrati (1) kaṭa kaṭa (2) maṭa maṭa (3) khiri kṣiṇa (4) kṣiṇa kṣiṇa (5) vañja vañja (6) namo cudrati (7) gurudhara (8) prajāye (9) svāhā (10) āvarta (11) min.
NAKṢATRA-CITTA-ĀH-SAMAGRA-CARATI (13) NAKṢIṆA-PANA-PRAGOPAYA (17) KURU KURU (18) JURU JURU (19) MURU MURU (20) NAMO NAMO (21) SVĀHĀ.
Recite this mantra— *Hā oṃ sara hūṃ svāhā*—
one hundred and eight times during each of the three periods of the day for three days and three nights, or even for seven days and seven nights,
while making offerings; then the manifested Nine-Eyed Heavenly King Kanabati will appear in accordance with one's form, like a shadow following a body.
The mantra master can drive [spirits] with his mind and manifest good and evil. Furthermore, those who uphold me in the highest degree shall become kings among men;
those who uphold me in the middle degree shall become teachers to kings; and those who uphold me in the lowest degree shall possess inexhaustible fortune and nobility.
Regarding all matters of good and evil, whatever one seeks or prays for will certainly be fulfilled without fail.
On the twenty-seventh day of the fifth month in the second year of An’gen, at the Hōjūji Hokkedō Monks’ Quarters,
in accordance with an imperial decree issued by the Court, this was presented and bestowed; it was transcribed from the Imperial manuscript and recorded by Ryōjin Eki.
